docs.title: Let The Fed be Fed
docs.desc: The U.S. now spends over $1 trillion a year just on interest, which gives politicians every reason to pressure the Fed to keep rates low. History shows how that ends: Arthur Burns gave in and got a decade of inflation, while Paul Volcker held firm and broke it. The real fix is a Congress that stops overspending. So does today's Fed have Volcker's nerve?
docs.body: Let The Fed be Fed The US national debt has crossed $40 trillion, and the government is on track to spend more than $1 trillion this year just on interest. The question is no longer whether this matters. It is who will have the nerve to act when it does. Rahul Saxena 9/25/2026 4 min read A central bank that flinches can't fix a debt crisis The US national debt has crossed $40 trillion , and the government is on track to spend more than $1 trillion this year just on interest . The question is no longer whether this matters. It is who will have the nerve to act when it does?That job falls to the Federal Reserve. The Fed has every right to intervene in the economy. But its decisions must be driven by economics, not by fear of angry politicians, election calendars, or market tantrums.When inflation calls for higher rates, the Fed should raise them without hesitation. Diplomacy has no place in monetary policy. Bandages on a growing cancer For two decades, Washington has treated every downturn with the same remedy: more borrowing, more bailouts, and cheaper money. Each round eased the pain for a while. None of them fixed the underlying disease. This is the core warning of the Austrian School. Artificially cheap credit keeps weak firms alive and lets bad investments pile up. Every rescue postpones the correction and makes the final reckoning larger.The damage is also psychological. docs.title: The Anxiety Trade
docs.desc: Oil near $95, 10-year yields at 4.8%, and a trillion-dollar AI spending spree all look scary, especially when strung together into one doomsday story. But they're separate, real risks, not a countdown clock. The market is sorting AI winners from losers exactly as it should. Uncertain isn't the same as doomed, so what's actually worth watching?
docs.body: The Anxiety Trade Every few years, the market finds a new way to convince itself the world is ending. Right now it's oil, bond yields, and the trillion-dollar question mark hanging over Silicon Valley's data centers. Rahul Saxena 9/2/2026 4 min read Every few years, the market finds a new way to convince itself the world is ending. Right now it's oil, bond yields, and the trillion-dollar question mark hanging over Silicon Valley's data centers. Individually, each of these is a legitimate worry. Strung together into one story, they start to sound like a countdown clock. They aren't. Start with oil, because that's where the fear actually has teeth. Brent crude is sitting around $95 a barrel, WTI near $91, both up roughly 40% from a year ago. That's not noise. But the headline explanation making the rounds â Ukraine choking off Russian exports, reserves running dry â isn't really what's moving the tape. The spike traces back to the Strait of Hormuz, where U.S. strikes on Iranian targets and retaliatory attacks on tankers have put a chokehold on one of the world's most important shipping lanes. Roughly a fifth of global oil supply moves through that strait. When traders get nervous about a chokepoint like that, prices don't creep â they jump. Does that mean $6 gas is coming? I wouldn't bet on it, at least not on the current trajectory. Getting there means oil somewhere north of $130 a barrel, which would require Hormuz to go from "tense" to genuinely closed, not just risky.

docs.title: The Machine That Doesn't Need Cheap Money
docs.desc: The Fed just raised rates, yet AI spending keeps growing because Big Tech pays for it with its own cash, not borrowed money. That has turned chips into a bargaining chip between the U.S. and China, while Europe absorbs an energy shock from the Iran war and the BRICS nations slowly gain influence. Right now these forces are pushing everyone toward the negotiating table, but for how long?
docs.body: The Machine That Doesn't Need Cheap Money The old story says hike rates and speculative excess gets squeezed out. It isn't playing out that way this time, at least not for artificial intelligence. Rahul Saxena 9/21/2026 5 min read There's a comfortable story that's been told for two years about the Fed and markets: hike rates, and speculative excess gets squeezed out. Sell the trade. Watch the leverage unwind. It's a story that worked reasonably well in 2022, and investors have been waiting for a sequel ever since. It isn't playing out that way this time, at least not for artificial intelligence. On September 16th, the Federal Reserve voted 12-0 to raise its target rate a quarter point, to a range of 3Â¾ to 4%. Sixteen of eighteen policymakers see another hike coming before the year is out. By the old playbook, that should be putting real pressure on the most speculative corner of the market â and AI, with its eye-watering capital commitments and uncertain near-term payoff, should be exhibit A. Instead, the number keeps getting bigger. Goldman Sachs now projects roughly $1 trillion in AI-related capital investment globally this year. JPMorgan and Goldman both see that figure climbing past $1 trillion again in 2027, with trillions more stacked up behind it. This isn't retail money chasing a meme. It's hyperscaler operating cash flow, sovereign wealth, pension allocations, private equity, and foreign capital, moving in a volume that dwarfs almost anything a quarter-point rate

docs.title: Right Fear, Wrong Reasons
docs.desc: Everyone is watching AI stocks and the next Fed meeting, but the real warning signs are in the financial system's plumbing. Consumers are tapped out, big investors are avoiding long-term bonds, young workers are stuck behind boomers who can't afford to retire, and high mortgage rates have frozen housing. Add it up, and the word that comes out isn't “soft landing.”
docs.body: Right Fear, Wrong Reasons We love the shiny objects: megacap tech, chip earnings, the next FOMC move. But the actual plumbing of the financial system is starting to clank, and the story it's telling isn't nearly as comfortable as the soft landing we've been sold. Rahul Saxena 9/25/2026 4 min read If you spend your time scrolling financial media, youâd think the entire global economy is just a daily referendum on artificial intelligence, semiconductor chips, and whatever the latest headline says about the Federal Reserve cutting or hiking next month. We love the shiny objects. We love tracking megacap tech valuations, dissecting earnings calls from chip designers, and arguing over whether a twenty-five-basis-point move is locked in for the next FOMC meeting. But while retail investors and cable news anchors stare blindly at the blinking green and red lights of the equity markets, the actual plumbing of the financial systemâthe short end of the yield curve, corporate liquidity channels, and institutional cash management desksâis starting to clank. And the story itâs telling isn't nearly as comfortable as the soft landing narrative weâve been sold. To understand why the foundation is shifting, we first have to admit a fundamental truth about how we measure economic weather: inflation has never been the neat, real-time data point economists pretend it is. docs.title: Nightmare on Bond Street
docs.desc: Bonds, the “safe” corner of finance, just had a scary stretch: the 30-year Treasury yield touched levels last seen in 2007 as U.S. debt crossed $40 trillion. The Treasury's answer, bigger bond buybacks, is a few billion dollars thrown at a $30 trillion market, and the Fed is staying quiet. Higher yields don't stay on Wall Street; they show up in mortgages, loans and prices. So how long will this Halloween last?
docs.body: Nightmare on Bond Street Halloween came early this year. Bonds, the boring corner of finance everyone parks their money in to sleep at night, have suddenly gotten a lot less boring. Rahul Saxena 8/25/2026 4 min read Halloween Came Early This Year (Thanks, Bond Market). Nothing says "spooky season" quite like watching yields climb and your portfolio turn red. Bonds â you know, the boring, "trusted and reliable" corner of finance everyone parks their money in when they want to sleep at night â have suddenly gotten a lot less boring. And not in a good way. So what's actually happening? Over the past few months, the 3-month bills, the 2-year note, and the 10 & 30-year bonds have all been gradually climbing. That's not unusual on its own. But last week, the 30-year touched levels last seen in 2007 â a 19-year high â while the 10-year hovered near its highest point in roughly 20 months. Not quite the 25-year record some headlines made it out to be, but still enough to make people sit up and pay attention. If you're holding anything on the long end of the curve, you've probably felt it. Higher duration means more sensitivity to rate moves, and right now that sensitivity is translating directly into red numbers. Meanwhile, corporate borrowing costs on investment-grade (IG) bonds are creeping up too â which is never a fun combo. What does this mean for the AI trade? Here's where it gets interesting. docs.title: The Welfare State Was Always a Ticking Clock. We're Just Now Hearing It Tick.
docs.desc: Welfare promises were made when many workers supported each retiree. Japan is down to about two, and the U.S. faces soaring healthcare costs and nearly $40 trillion in debt. Now AI could wipe out jobs just as those bills peak, forcing governments to spend even more, and opening a window for China. Is this just another cycle, or a countdown?
docs.body: The Welfare State Was Always a Ticking Clock. We're Just Now Hearing It Tick. Cradle-to-grave security sounded great on paper. Still does, in a stump speech. But paper doesn't have to pay pensions in 2050. People do. Rahul Saxena 8/30/2026 3 min read There's a version of the 20th century where the welfare state looks like a triumph â cradle-to-grave security, pensions for the elderly, healthcare as a right instead of a privilege. Sounded great on paper. Still does, in a stump speech. But paper doesn't have to pay pensions in 2050. People do. And the math on that is starting to look ugly almost everywhere you look. Take Japan. In the early '90s, something like six or seven working-age people supported every retiree. Comfortable margin. That's not a welfare state under strain, that's a party with an open bar and plenty of designated drivers. Fast forward to now and that ratio has collapsed to roughly two workers per retiree â Japan officially has the highest old-age dependency ratio in the world. Nobody voted to change the deal. Demographics just quietly rewrote it while everyone was looking at GDP numbers. Then there's Chile, which everyone name-drops without really sitting with the details. Salvador Allende took Chile hard toward socialism in the early '70s â nationalizing industries, land reform, the whole program â before the economy started buckling under inflation and shortages. docs.title: Bond Martinis, Shaken Not Stirred
docs.desc: Long-term Treasury yields are climbing, and the comforting idea that “the economy grows faster than our debt costs” is getting harder to believe. Higher yields lock the government into paying more interest for years, squeeze Big Tech's AI borrowing, and help explain gold's rally. It's not a five-alarm fire yet, but the ingredients for stagflation are on the table.
docs.body: Bond Martinis, Shaken Not Stirred Something's shifting in the bond market. Yields on longer-dated Treasuries have been climbing, and it's not a gentle drift. It's the kind of move that's rattling investors across the curve. Rahul Saxena 9/1/2026 3 min read Somethingâs shifting in the bond market, and if youâve been half-following the headlines,youâve probably felt it too. Yields on longer-dated Treasuries have been climbing, and itâs not a gentle drift â itâs the kind of move thatâs rattling investors and triggering real selloffs across the curve. So I sat down and worked through whatâs actually going on, and where I land on it. First, the reassurance everyone keeps repeating Thereâs a popular argument floating around that this isnât a big deal. The logic goes: as long as the economyâs nominal growth rate is still outrunning the yield on government debt,weâre fine. Think of it like a mortgage â if your income is growing faster than your interestrate, the loan gets easier to carry over time, even if you never touch the principal. Apply that to Uncle Sam, and the idea is the debt shrinks relative to the size of the economy almost on autopilot.Itâs a real thing, and historically itâs been the metric bond vigilantes watch closely. But hereâs the catch â that comfort only holds while growth stays above the yield. The moment yields start creeping up and closing that gap, or worse, crossing over it, the whole calming story flips into a warning sign.

docs.title: Accrued interest
docs.desc: Interest a bond has earned since its last payment date but hasn't paid out yet. When you buy a bond between payment dates, you pay the seller this amount on top of the price, because they held the bond for part of the period.
docs.body: A bond pays interest every six months. You buy it three months in, so you reimburse the seller for those three months of interest.

docs.title: Auction
docs.desc: How the U.S. government sells new Treasury debt. Big investors bid, and the bids decide the yield the government has to pay. Weak demand at an auction pushes yields up.

docs.title: Basis point
docs.desc: One hundredth of one percent (0.01%). Bond people use it to talk about small moves in rates without saying "point zero something."
docs.body: A yield rising from 4.50% to 4.75% is a 25 basis point move.

docs.title: Bear market (in bonds)
docs.desc: A period when bond prices fall, which means yields are rising. Bonds and yields always move in opposite directions.

docs.title: Benchmark yield
docs.desc: A widely watched yield that other borrowing costs are measured against. In the U.S. it is usually the 10-year Treasury yield, which strongly influences mortgage rates.

docs.title: Bid-to-cover ratio
docs.desc: At a Treasury auction, how much investors tried to buy compared with how much was on sale. A higher number means stronger demand.
docs.body: A ratio of 2.5 means buyers asked for $2.50 of bonds for every $1 on offer.

docs.title: Bond
docs.desc: A loan you make to a government or company. They promise to pay you interest along the way and return your money on a set date.

docs.title: Bond ladder
docs.desc: Owning several bonds that mature in different years, so some money comes back to you regularly and you are never stuck with just one interest rate.
docs.body: Bonds maturing in 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 years; each year one matures and you can reinvest it.

docs.title: Bond vigilantes
docs.desc: Investors who sell a government's bonds in protest when they think it is borrowing or spending recklessly. Their selling pushes yields up and makes more borrowing expensive.

docs.title: Bull market (in bonds)
docs.desc: A period when bond prices rise, which means yields are falling, usually because investors expect interest rates to drop.

docs.title: Callable bond
docs.desc: A bond the borrower is allowed to pay back early. Borrowers usually do this when rates fall, which is bad for you: you get your money back just when you can only reinvest it at lower rates.

docs.title: Carry
docs.desc: What you earn simply by holding a bond, its interest, minus what it costs to fund the position. A carry trade borrows cheap short-term money to buy higher-yielding bonds.

docs.title: Clean price / dirty price
docs.desc: The clean price is the quoted price of a bond. The dirty price is what you actually pay, which is the clean price plus accrued interest.

docs.title: Convexity
docs.desc: A refinement of duration. It captures the fact that a bond's price doesn't change in a perfectly straight line as rates move. For most everyday purposes, duration tells you enough.

docs.title: Corporate bond
docs.desc: A bond issued by a company rather than a government. It usually pays more than a Treasury because there is more risk the company can't pay.

docs.title: Coupon
docs.desc: The fixed interest a bond pays each year, shown as a percentage of its face value. The name comes from old paper bonds that had coupons you clipped and mailed in to get paid.
docs.body: A $1,000 bond with a 5% coupon pays $50 a year.

docs.title: Credit rating
docs.desc: A grade from an agency such as S&P, Moody's or Fitch on how likely a borrower is to pay back. AAA is the safest; anything below BBB- is considered junk.

docs.title: Credit risk
docs.desc: The risk that the borrower doesn't pay you the interest or your money back in full.

docs.title: Credit spread
docs.desc: How much extra yield a riskier bond pays compared with a safe government bond of similar length. Wider spreads mean investors are more nervous.
docs.body: A company bond yields 6% while the matching Treasury yields 4.5%: the spread is 1.5%, or 150 basis points.

docs.title: Current yield
docs.desc: A bond's yearly interest divided by its current market price. It is a quick snapshot and ignores any gain or loss you'll have when the bond matures.

docs.title: Default
docs.desc: When a borrower misses an interest payment or can't repay the loan. Bondholders may get back only part of their money, or nothing.

docs.title: Discount
docs.desc: When a bond's price is below its face value. This happens when its coupon is lower than current rates, so buyers pay less for it.
docs.body: A $1,000 bond selling for $950 is trading at a discount.

docs.title: Duration
docs.desc: A measure of how sensitive a bond's price is to changes in interest rates. The higher the duration, the more the price swings.
docs.body: A bond with a duration of 7 would fall roughly 7% if rates rose by 1 percentage point.

docs.title: Face value
docs.desc: The amount the borrower promises to repay when the bond matures, usually $1,000 per bond. Interest is calculated on this amount.

docs.title: Fallen angel
docs.desc: A bond that was investment grade but has been downgraded to junk. Many funds are required to sell these, which can push their prices down sharply.

docs.title: Fed funds rate
docs.desc: The short-term interest rate the Federal Reserve sets. When the Fed "raises rates" this is the rate it raises, and it ripples out to loans, savings accounts and bond yields.

docs.title: Fiscal dominance
docs.desc: When a government's debt is so large that the central bank feels pressured to keep interest rates low so the government can afford its interest bill, even if inflation says rates should go up.

docs.title: Fixed income
docs.desc: Another name for bonds and similar investments, because they typically pay a fixed, predictable amount of income.

docs.title: Floating-rate note
docs.desc: A bond whose interest payments go up and down with a benchmark rate, instead of staying fixed. Its price moves much less when rates change.

docs.title: High-yield bond
docs.desc: A bond rated below investment grade. It pays more interest to make up for a higher chance the borrower can't pay.

docs.title: Inflation risk
docs.desc: The risk that rising prices eat away the value of a bond's fixed payments. $50 a year buys less when everything costs more.

docs.title: Interest rate risk
docs.desc: The risk that rates rise and the value of the bonds you already own falls. The longer the bond, the bigger this risk.

docs.title: Inverted yield curve
docs.desc: When short-term bonds pay more than long-term bonds. It is unusual, and it has often come before recessions, because it suggests investors expect rates to fall.

docs.title: Investment grade
docs.desc: Bonds rated BBB- or higher, seen as relatively safe. Many pension funds and insurers are only allowed to own these.

docs.title: Issuer
docs.desc: The government, agency or company that borrows money by selling a bond.

docs.title: Liquidity
docs.desc: How easily you can buy or sell a bond quickly without moving its price much. Treasuries are very liquid; many small company or municipal bonds are not.

docs.title: Long end / short end
docs.desc: The long end is bonds that mature far in the future, such as 10 to 30 years. The short end is bonds that mature soon, from a few months to about two years.

docs.title: Maturity
docs.desc: The date the bond ends and the borrower must repay your money.

docs.title: Municipal bond
docs.desc: A bond issued by a U.S. state, city or local agency to pay for things like schools and roads. The interest is often free of federal income tax.

docs.title: Nominal yield
docs.desc: The yield before adjusting for inflation. The yield you see quoted is almost always nominal.

docs.title: Premium
docs.desc: When a bond's price is above its face value. This happens when its coupon is higher than current rates, so buyers pay extra for it.

docs.title: Primary / secondary market
docs.desc: The primary market is where new bonds are first sold by the issuer. The secondary market is where investors buy and sell existing bonds from each other afterwards.

docs.title: Principal
docs.desc: The original amount lent, which is paid back at maturity. For most bonds it is the same as the face value.

docs.title: Quantitative easing
docs.desc: When a central bank buys large amounts of bonds to push down long-term interest rates and pump money into the financial system.

docs.title: Quantitative tightening
docs.desc: The reverse of QE: the central bank shrinks its bond holdings, which tends to push long-term rates up.

docs.title: Real yield
docs.desc: A bond's yield minus inflation: what you actually earn in buying power.
docs.body: A 4.5% yield with 3% inflation is roughly a 1.5% real yield.

docs.title: Refinancing
docs.desc: Paying off old debt by issuing new debt. When old debt was borrowed cheaply and new rates are higher, refinancing raises the borrower's interest bill.

docs.title: Reinvestment risk
docs.desc: The risk that when a bond pays you interest or matures, you can only reinvest that money at lower rates than before.

docs.title: Repo
docs.desc: A very short-term loan, often overnight, where one party sells bonds and agrees to buy them back the next day at a slightly higher price. It is a key piece of the financial system's plumbing.

docs.title: Seniority
docs.desc: Your place in line if a company goes bust. Senior bondholders get paid back before junior (subordinated) ones, and all bondholders come before shareholders.

docs.title: Sovereign bond
docs.desc: A bond issued by a national government, such as U.S. Treasuries, German Bunds or Japanese JGBs.

docs.title: Stagflation
docs.desc: The painful mix of weak economic growth and high inflation at the same time. It is hard to fix, because the usual cure for one makes the other worse.

docs.title: Steepening / flattening
docs.desc: Describes the gap between long-term and short-term yields. Steepening means the gap is widening; flattening means it is shrinking.

docs.title: Term premium
docs.desc: The extra yield investors demand for locking their money up for a long time instead of rolling over short-term bonds.

docs.title: TIPS
docs.desc: U.S. government bonds whose principal rises with inflation, so your payments keep their buying power.

docs.title: Treasury bills, notes and bonds
docs.desc: U.S. government debt, named by length. Bills mature in a year or less, notes in 2 to 10 years, and bonds in 20 or 30 years.

docs.title: Yield
docs.desc: The return you get from a bond, shown as a yearly percentage. When bond prices fall, yields rise, and vice versa, like two ends of a seesaw.

docs.title: Yield curve
docs.desc: A chart of yields for bonds of different lengths, from short to long. Normally it slopes upward, because lending for longer usually pays more.

docs.title: Yield to maturity
docs.desc: The total yearly return you'd earn if you bought a bond today at its current price and held it until it matures, counting both its interest and any gain or loss on price.

docs.title: Zero-coupon bond
docs.desc: A bond that pays no interest along the way. You buy it at a deep discount and get the full face value back at maturity; the difference is your return.
docs.body: Pay $780 today, get $1,000 back in five years.

docs.title: Introduction: Bonds, Futures and Options
docs.desc: What a bond is, why its price moves when rates change, and how traders use bond futures and options.

docs.title: A Short History of Bonds
docs.desc: From clay tablets in Mesopotamia to a $40 trillion U.S. debt: how lending to governments shaped the world.

docs.title: Classification of Bonds
docs.desc: Treasuries, corporates, mortgage bonds, CBOs, private equity debt, and how ratings from AAA to D work.

docs.title: Cash Logistics
docs.desc: Follow $1,000 from your account to the borrower, into the economy, and back to you as interest and principal.

docs.title: Bond Dictionary
docs.desc: 60 bond terms explained in everyday language, from basis points to yield curves.

docs.title: The Players
docs.desc: Interactive charts of the $61 trillion U.S. bond market, who owns the national debt, and the giants who move it.

docs.title: Fortunes Made and Lost
docs.desc: A king who stiffed his bankers, a county that bet the treasury, Nobel winners and a 100-year bond: the bond market’s greatest wins and wipeouts.

docs.title: U.S. Treasuries
docs.desc: Debt issued by the U.S. government. Backed by the government's ability to tax, they are treated as the safest dollar investment and the benchmark every other bond is priced against.
docs.keys: Treasury bills (T-bills), Treasury notes (T-notes), Treasury bonds (T-bonds), TIPS, Floating-rate notes (FRNs), STRIPS, Savings bonds (I bonds, EE bonds)
docs.body: Short-term, maturing in a year or less. They pay no interest along the way; you buy them below face value and get the full amount back at maturity. Medium-term: 2, 3, 5, 7 or 10 years. They pay interest every six months. The 10-year note is the most watched interest rate in the world. Long-term: 20 or 30 years, paying interest every six months. Their prices swing the most when rates move. Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities. The principal rises with inflation, so the interest you receive keeps its buying power. Two-year Treasuries whose interest resets every week with T-bill rates, so their price barely moves when rates change. Treasuries split into separate pieces, one for each interest payment and one for the principal, and sold individually as zero-coupon bonds. Sold directly to individuals, not traded in the market. I bonds track inflation; EE bonds are guaranteed to double in value if held for 20 years.

docs.title: Other public-sector bonds
docs.desc: Bonds from government-linked borrowers that aren't the Treasury itself.
docs.keys: Agency bonds, Municipal bonds (munis), Sovereign bonds
docs.body: Issued by government-sponsored agencies such as Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the Federal Home Loan Banks. Very safe, and they pay slightly more than Treasuries. Issued by states, cities and local authorities. General-obligation munis are backed by taxes; revenue munis are paid from a specific project, such as a toll road. Interest is often free of federal income tax. National government debt from other countries, such as German Bunds, UK gilts or Japanese JGBs. Risk depends on the country and on the currency the bond is in.

docs.title: Corporate bonds
docs.desc: Companies borrow from investors instead of a bank. They pay more than Treasuries because a company can go bust.
docs.keys: Investment grade, High yield (junk), Secured vs. unsecured, Senior vs. subordinated, Callable bonds, Convertible bonds, Commercial paper
docs.body: Bonds from financially strong companies, rated BBB- or higher. Lower risk, lower yield. Bonds rated below BBB-. They pay more because the risk of default is higher. Often used to fund leveraged buyouts. Secured bonds are backed by specific assets, such as property or equipment, that bondholders can claim in a default. Unsecured bonds (debentures) rely only on the company's promise. Senior bondholders are paid back first if the company fails; subordinated holders only after them, so they earn more to make up for it. The company can repay early, usually when rates fall, which caps your upside. Bonds that can be swapped for the company's shares, giving you a slice of the upside if the stock rises. Very short-term company IOUs, usually under 270 days, used to cover day-to-day cash needs.

docs.title: Mortgage-backed securities (MBS)
docs.desc: Thousands of home loans are pooled together, and investors buy bonds paid by the monthly mortgage payments flowing through the pool.
docs.keys: Agency MBS, Non-agency (private-label) MBS, Prepayment risk, CMOs, CMBS
docs.body: Guaranteed by Ginnie Mae (backed by the U.S. government) or by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Credit risk is low; the main risk is timing. Pools put together by banks without a government guarantee. These were at the center of the 2008 crisis. When rates fall, homeowners refinance and pay off early, so investors get their money back just when they can only reinvest it at lower rates. Collateralized mortgage obligations split a pool's payments into slices (tranches) with different maturities and risks. The same idea for commercial property loans: offices, malls, hotels and warehouses.

docs.title: Asset-backed and structured bonds
docs.desc: Bonds built from pools of other loans or bonds, sliced by risk.
docs.keys: ABS, CBO (collateralized bond obligation), CLO (collateralized loan obligation), CDO
docs.body: Asset-backed securities paid by pools of car loans, credit-card balances, student loans or equipment leases. A pool of corporate bonds, often high yield, sold to investors in tranches. The senior tranche is paid first and is safest; the equity tranche is paid last and absorbs losses first. The same structure built from leveraged loans to companies. Today CLOs are far larger than CBOs. The umbrella name for these structures. CDOs packed with risky mortgage bonds were a major cause of the 2008 financial crisis.

docs.title: Private equity and private credit
docs.desc: Private equity firms buy companies using a lot of borrowed money, and a whole corner of the bond market has grown up around them.
docs.keys: Buyout (LBO) debt, Private equity firm bonds, Collateralized fund obligations (CFOs), NAV loans and rated feeder notes, Private credit
docs.body: When a private equity firm buys a company, most of the price is often borrowed by the company itself through high-yield bonds and leveraged loans. The company, not the firm, owes the debt. Large listed firms such as KKR, Apollo and Blackstone issue their own corporate bonds, often rated investment grade, backed by their fee income. Bonds backed by stakes in a portfolio of private equity funds. Investors are repaid from the cash those funds distribute over time. Borrowing against the value of a fund's holdings, or notes that let insurers invest in private funds in bond form. Newer, less transparent and harder to sell. Loans made directly by funds to companies, outside the public bond market. Fast-growing, and less regulated and less visible than traded bonds.
